rv.q: August Wilson's gift for storytelling has rarely been more beguiling than in this lyrical 1986 drama, and in his searing revival, director Bartlett Sher makes every note strong and true.
For the essence of this production is in its organic acting, which matches Mr. Wilson’s writing in its melding of the quotidian and the cosmic.

They are searching for his long-missing wife. Bynum (the puckishly powerful Roger Robinson) has the power to "bind" people together. He is a link to an Africa that separation has mutated into its own American thing.
But it's because of Sher that Herald, Coleman, and the rest of Wilson's brilliant play never shine as brightly as they should.
The ensemble of actors takes that message to heart, delivering performances that define each character as a distinct individual but also one of a shared community.

cn.t: Wilson's masterwork receives a splendid revival that feels airborne despite heavy themes, with critics praising Sher's ethereal direction and the play's poetic power. One dissenter finds it less successful, but most hail this as a triumphant return to Broadway.

sg.ra: Belasco was designed by David Belasco as a 'living room' with a shallow depth to support the Little Theater movement's emphasis on actor-audience proximity. Center Orchestra rows B-D sit at the ideal distance (reviewers cite row B as the fourth row from stage at 'perfect distance') with head-on actor views. Mezzanine overhang begins at row J per SeatPlan, so rows BB-H stay clear.

SeatPlan confirms 'The Mezzanine overhang begins at row J, meaning seats behind this may experience cut-off at the top of the stage.' Rows J-Q trade top-of-stage visibility for lower prices. Headout and TickPick both flag G-P/F-O center as value picks. Row N's extra legroom offsets the overhang compromise for tall patrons.

SeatPlan: 'Seats at the Left and Right edges suffer from restricted views of the stage,' particularly corner seats in rows B-E. TickPick confirms 'Far Left/Right Orchestra: Angled views may occur.' Historic box configuration and shallow house geometry amplify side-angle distortion.

sg.vl: Aerial sweet spot, skip row A
sg.ra: Mezzanine hangs close and center row C delivers aerial perspective with decent rake. Row A is a common trap: 'Mezzanine row A seat 111 was obstructed view, and the rail literally blocks half of the stage' (Tripadvisor user report). Balcony overhang begins at mezz row C per SeatPlan, so rows A-B stay open-topped but row A's safety bar offsets that benefit.

Headout flags F-H center as the mezzanine value range. Balcony overhang starting at row C means rows E-H sit under it — top of set may be cut. Side mezzanine suffers progressively more restricted angles 'due to stage curvature' (SeatPlan). Acceptable for dialogue-heavy work but not flown spectacle.

Center Balcony 'extends back six rows on a steep rake which provides a bird's-eye-view of the stage' (SeatPlan). Rows B-D balance price and sightline. Distance is the honest tradeoff: AVFMS reviewer on Maybe Happy Ending noted 'the real problem is how far back the balcony is. You'll have to lean forward to see for most of the show.' Row A safety rail can also obstruct.

sg.vl: Up to 1/3 of stage cut off
sg.ra: SeatPlan: 'the curve of the section and other features including the Left Boxes may cut off up to a third of the stage at the outside.' Combined with steep rake, distance, and row A rail, side balcony is the worst seat class in the house. Historic 1907 box architecture is the root cause — it cannot be engineered out per production.
